name: Sciton BBL / Moxi / Halo

lead: BBL, Moxi and Halo are treatments on Sciton platforms: broadband light, a light fractional 1927-nm laser and a deeper hybrid fractional laser. Clinics sometimes combine them in a session to address sun damage, pigment, redness, texture and scars for a fresher, more even complexion.

BBL uses filtered flashlamp light on pigment and vessels. Moxi and Halo create tiny columns of controlled injury so skin renews and remodels. Published work naming them is small: a completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment, and a 2023 study examined fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes.

paras: These are clinic procedures, often chosen in combination, with the depth set by the provider. Light settings carry short recovery, while deeper Halo settings mean more healing time. Results build over weeks as skin renews.
Listed concerns include pigment change after laser, healing time with deeper resurfacing, and that these are clinic-only procedures. Darker skin carries higher pigment-change risk.

angle.text: BBL clears pigment and redness with light, while Moxi and Halo resurface with fractional laser, leaving a smoother, more even complexion. People combine them for sun damage, texture and scars, and supporting studies are small pilots.

lead: BBL, Moxi and Halo are treatments performed on laser and light platforms made by Sciton. BBL (BroadBand Light) is an intense pulsed light treatment, Moxi is a fractionated 1927-nm laser, and Halo is a dual-wavelength 2940/1470-nm hybrid fractional laser, as described by the titles of registered studies.[1][1] They are used for photoaging, pigment, redness, texture and scars, and are sometimes combined in one session.[1]

Evidence is a mix of small studies. A completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for skin pigment[1], a split-face study compared IPL with pulsed dye laser for facial erythema[2], and a 2023 study examined fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes.[3] Many older Sciton papers concern erbium:YAG resurfacing.
infobox: Light and laser treatments on Sciton platforms
BBL (IPL), Moxi (1927 nm fractional), Halo (2940/1470 nm hybrid fractional)

paras: BBL is a broadband, non-laser light source of the intense pulsed light type, which uses filtered flashlamp light to target pigment or blood vessels.[4] A split-face comparison found IPL could be used in place of pulsed dye laser for reducing facial erythema.[2]

Moxi is described in registered studies as a fractionated 1927-nm laser for pigmentation and photodamage.[1][3] Fractionated resurfacing treats a pattern of microscopic columns and leaves surrounding skin intact.
Halo is described as a dual-wavelength 2940/1470 nm hybrid fractional laser.[1][5] A recruiting trial evaluates a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in patients with skin of colour.[5]

Studies of ablative erbium and CO2 resurfacing report differences in healing time and side-effect rates, and trials of wound dressings after fractional erbium resurfacing show post-procedure care is an active area of study.[6][7] Laser-induced hyperpigmentation is listed as a condition in one registered trial.[5]

A completed 15-participant trial combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment (NCT06091215), a 38-participant phase 4 trial examined a moisturiser with a non-ablative laser for photoaging, and a 5-participant study evaluated infrared and broadband light for skin ageing.[1][8][9] A study of fractionated 1927-nm laser reported on diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes.[3] Single-pass CO2 and multiple-pass Er:YAG resurfacing were directly compared for healing and side effects in an older trial.[6] Sample sizes are small and registry entries here do not summarise results.
